title: Cyber Defenders Unit 6 · The Defender's toolkit (6-8)

items.q: An account's passphrase is phished in a fake page. Which layer is designed to stop the attacker next?
choices: Two-step sign-in, which the fake page does not have
items.why: The phished passphrase is already gone. Two-step sign-in asks for a second proof that the fake page never got.

items.q: What is the difference between a vulnerability and a threat?
choices: A vulnerability is a flaw that can be used; a threat is who or what might use it
A threat is a kind of update
A vulnerability only exists on paper
items.why: They are different: a vulnerability is a flaw, and a threat is who or what might use that flaw.

items.q: Build the stack for a scenario account used for school projects. Which setup is defense in depth?
choices: One very long passphrase and nothing else
Updates on, a unique passphrase, two-step sign-in, and a backup
A passphrase written on a sticker for safety
Backups only, with no sign-in at all
items.why: Defense in depth stacks layers: updates, a unique passphrase, two-step sign-in and a backup. One layer alone is not depth.

items.q: A delivery note is secretly edited in transit, so the parcel goes to the wrong house. Which promise broke?
choices: Integrity: the information did not stay correct
items.why: The note was changed on the way, so the information is no longer correct. That is integrity, not secrecy or reachability.

items.q: Who enforces a school's acceptable use policy, and who enforces the law?
choices: The school enforces its policy; the law is enforced by the legal system
items.why: Each layer has its own enforcer: the school enforces its policy, and the legal system enforces the law.

items.q: Which part of an app's terms is doing a job that protects the user?
choices: The clause promising an appeal route when content is removed
The clause with the longest words
items.why: An appeal route protects users when their content is removed. Logos, addresses and long words do no job for the user.

items.q: What is the professional incident drill, in order?
items.why: First contain the damage, then preserve evidence, then report, then recover. Recovering first can destroy the proof.

items.q: Why preserve screenshots and times instead of deleting the message in embarrassment?
choices: Evidence lets adults and the platform act; deletion destroys the proof
Deletion is a report by itself
items.why: Adults and platforms act on evidence. Deleting in embarrassment destroys the proof they would need.

items.q: You clicked a faked sender's link and typed your passphrase, then realized. Run the whole drill: what comes first and last?
choices: First report to the whole internet, last preserve
First contain from a clean device, last recover with new passphrases everywhere the old one was reused
First delete everything, last say nothing
items.why: Contain first, from a clean device, so the thief is shut out. Recover last, with new passphrases wherever the old one was used.

items.q: Inside the escape room, one lock offers a second proof of who you are before it opens. Which idea is that?
choices: Two-step sign-in: a second, different proof
items.why: A second, different proof of who you are before a lock opens is two-step sign-in.

items.q: A lock's message wears Pim's name, but its real address is a stranger's and it begs for your key. What is it?
choices: Spoofing: a claimed sender in costume
items.why: A friendly name over a stranger's address, begging for your key, is spoofing: a claimed sender in costume.

items.q: The Which Pim? lock shows two messages. One repeats a public post word for word; the other answers a private delivery question correctly. Which clue matters?
choices: What each sender could only know if the footprint and the facts line up
The message with the festival poster
items.why: Length and posters prove nothing. What matters is what each sender could only know if the footprint and facts line up.
